name: Billy the Kid
kicker: Outlaw of the Lincoln County War · Killed by Sheriff Pat Garrett in 1881
briefing: Billy the Kid was born Henry McCarty, probably in New York City, and also went by Henry Antrim and William H. Bonney. As a teenager in New Mexico Territory, he joined one side of a deadly feud called the Lincoln County War and became a wanted outlaw. Sheriff Pat Garrett captured him in 1880; after Billy escaped from jail, killing two deputies, Garrett tracked him down and shot him at Fort Sumner on July 14, 1881.
answerHtml: Billy the Kid (accept Henry McCarty, William H. Bonney, or Henry Antrim; prompt on Kid or Billy)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: As a teenager in Silver City, New Mexico Territory, this future outlaw was jailed for holding a bundle of stolen laundry, and he escaped by climbing up the jail’s chimney. His mother had died of tuberculosis there the year before.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw who was shot and killed by Sheriff Pat Garrett in 1881.

tossups.p: In 1877, near Camp Grant in Arizona Territory, this young man shot and killed a blacksmith named Frank “Windy” Cahill during a fight, then fled to New Mexico. There he later went to work for the English rancher John Tunstall.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw of the Lincoln County War who was later killed by Pat Garrett.

tossups.p: This young ranch hand joined a group called the Regulators after a sheriff’s posse killed his employer, John Tunstall, in February 1878. Tunstall and the lawyer Alexander McSween had challenged the business owners known as “the House,” led by James Dolan.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw who fought in the resulting Lincoln County War and was later killed by Pat Garrett.

tossups.p: On April 1, 1878, Sheriff William Brady was killed in an ambush on the main street of Lincoln by a group of gunmen that included this man. Three years later, a court in Mesilla [“meh-SEE-yuh”] convicted this man of Brady’s murder and sentenced him to hang.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw of the Lincoln County War, later killed by Sheriff Pat Garrett.

tossups.p: In July 1878, this man was among the fighters trapped inside Alexander McSween’s house during a five-day gun battle in the town of Lincoln. When the house was set on fire, he escaped into the night, but McSween was killed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this young outlaw of the Lincoln County War who was later hunted down by Pat Garrett.

tossups.p: In March 1879, this man met secretly with a territorial governor who was then writing the novel _Ben-Hur_. He agreed to testify about the killing of the lawyer Huston Chapman in exchange for a pardon, but the pardon never came.
tossups.r: That governor was Lew Wallace. For 10 points, name this outlaw who was killed by Pat Garrett in 1881.

tossups.p: In December 1880, Governor Lew Wallace offered a $500 reward for this outlaw’s capture. That same month, a posse surrounded this man’s gang in a small stone building at Stinking Springs, killed Charlie Bowdre, and forced the rest to surrender.
tossups.r: That posse was led by Sheriff Pat Garrett. For 10 points, name this outlaw whom Garrett later killed.

tossups.p: On April 28, 1881, this prisoner, who was awaiting execution, escaped from the Lincoln County courthouse after killing his two guards, deputies James Bell and Robert Olinger. He rode away and returned to his friends near Fort Sumner.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw whom Pat Garrett tracked down and killed less than three months later.

tossups.p: This man’s last words, spoken in a darkened bedroom at Fort Sumner, are usually given as “¿Quién es?” (Spanish for “Who is it?”). That bedroom belonged to Pete Maxwell, whom a sheriff had come to question about this man’s whereabouts.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw shot and killed by Pat Garrett on July 14, 1881.

tossups.p: This man is buried at Fort Sumner beside two friends, Tom O’Folliard and Charlie Bowdre, under a shared stone marked “Pals.” His own gravestone has been stolen more than once, and the graves are protected by a metal cage.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw killed by Sheriff Pat Garrett in 1881, when he was about 21.

tossups.p: In 2011, a tintype photograph of this man taken around 1880 sold at auction for $2.3 million. Because tintypes show a mirror image, people long believed he was left-handed, an idea used in the title of a 1958 Paul Newman film.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw of the Lincoln County War, killed by Pat Garrett in 1881.

tossups.p: In 1882, a sheriff published a book about this man that was largely ghostwritten by the sheriff’s friend Ash Upson and helped spread many legends. One legend claimed this man had killed 21 men, one for each year of his life, though historians count far fewer.
tossups.r: That sheriff was Pat Garrett. For 10 points, name this outlaw whom Garrett had killed the year before.

tossups.p: In 1950, a Texas man named Brushy Bill Roberts claimed to be this outlaw, saying he had survived and lived for decades under another name. In 2010, New Mexico governor Bill Richardson decided not to grant this outlaw a pardon that had been promised long before.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw whom Sheriff Pat Garrett killed at Fort Sumner in 1881.

tossups.p: Eugene Loring created the dances for a 1938 ballet about this outlaw for Lincoln Kirstein’s company, Ballet Caravan. That ballet’s score quotes cowboy songs and includes a section called “Gun Battle.” It begins and ends with music picturing the open prairie.
tossups.r: Its composer was Aaron Copland. For 10 points, name this outlaw who was killed by Pat Garrett.

tossups.p: Emilio Estevez played this outlaw in the 1988 film _Young Guns_, and Kris Kristofferson played him in a 1973 Sam Peckinpah Western whose soundtrack, by Bob Dylan, includes “Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door.” A ballad about him appears on _Piano Man_, an album released that same year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this outlaw who was shot by Sheriff Pat Garrett in 1881 at Fort Sumner, New Mexico.

trap.title: Which name? Which Kid?
trap.body: This outlaw used several names: he was born Henry McCarty, went by Henry Antrim (his stepfather’s last name) as a teenager, and later called himself William H. Bonney. Answer lines accept all of them. Don’t confuse him with other Western “Kids,” like the Sundance Kid (Butch Cassidy’s partner) or the made-up Cisco Kid, or with Pat Garrett, the sheriff who killed him.
trap.fix: Lincoln County, John Tunstall, Lew Wallace, Fort Sumner, and Pat Garrett mean Billy the Kid. The Sundance Kid robbed trains with Butch Cassidy’s Wild Bunch and is believed to have died in Bolivia. If the question asks for “this sheriff” or “this lawman,” the answer is Pat Garrett.
trap.line: Real answer line: Billy the Kid (accept Henry McCarty, William H. Bonney, or Henry Antrim; prompt on Kid or Billy)
